title: The Toggle at 01:17

scenes.q: Mira can stop the location stream before release, but the manager wants to ship now. Which launch plan properly addresses the missing permission?
scenes.a: Explain location collection and its purpose, then obtain affirmative consent before enabling the new location stream.
scenes.why: Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, signified by clear affirmative action. The notice must describe the personal data and purpose.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 6(1)–(2); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3
bad: Explain location collection and its purpose, then interpret continued browsing as consent to the location stream.
Obtain device location permission before collection, then provide the service purpose when users open account settings.
Explain location collection and partner promotions, then require one combined approval before enabling the location stream.
scenes.plot: PulseStep’s new nearby-classes feature requests location the moment the app opens. A tester flags that the permission appears before anyone sees what the location is for.
scenes.good: The location stream waits for a meaningful choice. Mira keeps the release in staging.
scenes.effect: Location flows before users understand it. Mira finds coordinates in the release logs.

scenes.q: Marketing has the class-alert numbers and a campaign ready to send. No new consent or specific lawful use has been established. Which instruction should you approve?
scenes.a: Hold the campaign until customers receive the new purpose notice and provide consent for promotional messages.
scenes.why: Personal data may be processed for a lawful purpose for which consent was given or for certain legitimate uses set out in the Act. A delivery notice does not itself authorize promotional use.
bad: Send the new purpose notice before launch, then include customers who leave their existing preferences unchanged.
Keep the campaign within the company, then use class-alert consent to authorize messages about premium memberships.
Approve a restricted partner contract before launch, then use existing class-alert numbers for the promotional campaign.
scenes.plot: At 01:42, marketing asks to reuse the phone numbers collected for class alerts to sell premium memberships. Same customers, new purpose, same deadline.
scenes.good: The delivery list stays out of the promotion queue. Marketing discovers the existence of purposes.
scenes.effect: Delivery numbers enter a promotional campaign. Customers learn their courier has become a salesperson.

scenes.q: The partner will fund the release only if safety alerts and promotions share a checkbox. Which redesign preserves a meaningful choice?
scenes.a: Describe each purpose with separate controls, allowing customers to approve safety alerts while declining partner promotions.
scenes.why: Consent must be specific and informed, and the notice should clearly describe the purpose. Combining unrelated purposes undermines meaningful choice.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 6(1); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3
bad: Describe each purpose with separate headings, requiring customers to approve safety alerts together with partner promotions.
Describe each purpose with separate controls, enabling both initially and allowing customers to change preferences afterward.
Describe each purpose with separate explanations, treating approval of safety alerts as authorization for partner promotions.
scenes.plot: An ad partner offers to fund the feature if safety alerts and promotions share one checkbox. Product says separate choices will lower conversions.
scenes.good: Separate controls survive launch. Users can receive safety alerts without sponsoring an ad exchange.
scenes.effect: One checkbox forces unrelated uses together. The consent trail cannot show a specific choice for advertising.

speaker: MIRA / QA
brief: A fitness launch is harvesting more than steps. Follow the permissions to the advertising exchange.
joke: The button says Allow. The roadmap says allow everything.

title: The Permission That Wouldn’t Leave

scenes.q: Mira still needs her account, but her identifier remains in the offers export after withdrawal. Which fix respects the choice she actually made?
scenes.a: Stop offer processing through an equally easy withdrawal route, while continuing core services with independent justification.
scenes.why: A Data Principal may withdraw consent at any time, with ease comparable to giving it. The Act does not require withdrawal from one purpose to end unrelated processing that has its own lawful basis.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 6(4)–(6); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3(c)
bad: Stop collecting new offer data through immediate withdrawal, while retaining existing profiles until the campaign expires.
Remove the offer preference immediately, while requiring closure of the core account before stopping offer processing.
Keep core services active and stop offer processing once support validates the signed withdrawal form manually.
scenes.plot: Mira withdraws permission for personalized offers but wants to keep using her account. A retention dashboard marks her as a churn risk.
scenes.good: Personalised offers stop; separately justified account functions keep working.
scenes.effect: Mira’s choice is ignored or her whole account is unnecessarily destroyed. Neither respects her specific request.

scenes.q: Support can simplify only one withdrawal release tonight. Which plan fixes both the unclear notice and the nine-screen barrier?
scenes.a: Clarify the notice and introduce a straightforward withdrawal control, with verification proportionate to the actual request.
scenes.why: The Rules require notice in clear and plain language, independently understandable, with links or means to withdraw consent, exercise rights and make complaints.
bad: Clarify the notice and retain the existing withdrawal sequence, with verification repeated across its nine screens.
Clarify the notice and publish a support address, with withdrawal accepted after the existing sequence finishes.
Clarify the notice and introduce direct withdrawal for subscribers, with other users following the support-assisted route.
scenes.plot: The settings team reveals that withdrawal takes nine screens, while giving permission took one tap. Support has already received complaints.
scenes.good: Withdrawal becomes as easy as consent. Support closes the maze-related tickets.
scenes.effect: The withdrawal obstacle course keeps processing alive after the user tries to stop it.

scenes.q: Mira needs to manage choices across several providers. Which service model satisfies that role without substituting its own purposes?
scenes.a: Choose a registered manager offering accessible, transparent, interoperable consent controls, acting on behalf of its users.
scenes.why: The Act defines a Consent Manager as a person registered with the Board who acts as a single point of contact to enable a Data Principal to give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.
bad: Choose an interoperable manager offering accessible, transparent consent controls, completing Board registration after the service launches.
Choose a registered manager offering accessible consent controls, using customer choices to build its advertising profiles.
Choose a registered manager offering transparent consent controls, limiting customer choices to its own affiliated providers.
scenes.plot: Mira asks for one place to review permissions she gave to several services. A partner offers a consent dashboard but wants to use it for ad targeting too.
scenes.good: Mira gets a route through a registered Consent Manager, accountable to her.
scenes.effect: An unregistered intermediary acquires permissions it cannot manage as a statutory Consent Manager.

speaker: MIRA / CUSTOMER
brief: An opt-out exposes a retention machine. Help one person reclaim control without losing the service.
joke: Our unsubscribe journey has nine screens. The hero’s journey only had twelve.

title: The Form That Ate the City

scenes.q: The grant deadline is near and the vendor offers encryption for every extra field. Which collection plan fits the application’s stated purpose?
scenes.a: Retain fields necessary for stated eligibility checks, and remove unrelated collection before opening the application portal.
scenes.why: The Act requires processing for a lawful purpose and its consent framework requires a specific purpose. Data collection should match that purpose; unrelated data is not justified by convenience.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, ss. 4 and 6(1); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3
bad: Encrypt fields collected beyond eligibility checks, and reserve them for departmental requests after opening the portal.
Retain mandatory contact uploads alongside eligibility checks, and defer inspection until a departmental need becomes clearer.
Retain browsing history under fraud-prevention consent, and define its specific eligibility role after the application launch.
scenes.plot: A city grant portal asks applicants for eligibility documents, full contact lists, and unrelated browsing history. The vendor says extra fields will make future fraud checks easier.
scenes.good: The form asks only for relevant eligibility information. Applicants keep unrelated data to themselves.
scenes.effect: Applicants surrender unrelated data for a grant. The portal creates exposure without a justified purpose.

scenes.q: Another department might use the extra records next year, but nobody can specify why today. What must you require before approving collection?
scenes.a: Require a specific lawful purpose and a permitted processing basis before approving collection of additional records.
scenes.why: The Act permits processing for a lawful purpose, based on consent or a certain legitimate use. A vague possible future use is not itself a stated purpose.
bad: Require a documented future benefit and provisional departmental approval before approving collection of the additional records.
Require encryption and restricted departmental access before approving collection, with the processing purpose finalized after launch.
Require broad applicant agreement to departmental use before approving collection, with specific purposes assigned during review.
scenes.plot: A new analyst proposes keeping every field because another department may someday find it useful. No present purpose is written in the launch brief.
scenes.good: Speculative collection stops until a lawful, specific purpose and basis exist.
scenes.effect: The city accumulates data for an imaginary future use. Maybe later is not a lawful ground.

scenes.q: The official requester has been authenticated, but the legal function and needed fields remain unclear. Which response should the team make?
scenes.a: Confirm the applicable legal ground, statutory function and necessary fields before approving the authenticated office request.
scenes.why: The Act permits processing for certain legitimate uses, including specified functions under law, subject to statutory conditions. A public authority should identify the applicable ground rather than assume every government use is automatically permitted.
bad: Confirm the requesting office and secure transfer route before approving all fields in its authenticated request.
Confirm the sharing agreement and recipient safeguards before treating government status as sufficient grounds for disclosure.
Confirm the original grant consent and requester identity before applying that consent to subsequent departmental requests.
scenes.plot: A public office sends a request for records needed to perform a function imposed by law. The request is broad and cites no specific function.
scenes.good: The office identifies the statutory function and conditions before processing.
scenes.effect: An official letter becomes an unlimited request. Government status cannot justify every use.

speaker: DEV / CITY OPS
brief: A grant application grows tentacles. Trace its data appetite from one form to a government request.
joke: Fraud prevention needs your aunt’s contacts. Apparently fraud has an aunt.

title: The Schoolyard Signal

scenes.q: The ad module profiles children and no applicable exemption has been established. Which plan addresses both consent and the separate restrictions?
scenes.a: Verify parental consent before processing, and disable child tracking, behavioral monitoring and targeted advertising before release.
scenes.why: The Act defines a child as a person under 18. Before processing a child’s personal data, verifiable parental consent is required; tracking, behavioral monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children are restricted, subject to prescribed exceptions.
bad: Verify parental consent before processing, and retain child behavioral profiling within the advertising settings parents approve.
Disable targeted advertising before release, and accept the child’s own agreement for the remaining personal-data collection.
Replace names with persistent identifiers before release, and retain child tracking within the protected advertising module.
scenes.plot: A learning game’s new ad module tracks how children pause, replay, and abandon lessons. The growth team calls it ordinary product analytics.
scenes.good: Behavioural advertising stops. Applicable child protections and verifiable parental consent are checked.
scenes.effect: Children become behavioural advertising targets. A free game does not remove protection.

scenes.q: The sixteen-year-old clicked Accept, but no verified guardian consent or applicable exemption is recorded. Which instruction should you approve?
scenes.a: Pause processing until verifiable parental or guardian consent is obtained for the sixteen-year-old’s personal data collection.
scenes.why: A child is an individual under 18, and section 9 generally requires verifiable parental or guardian consent before processing a child’s personal data.
bad: Record the sixteen-year-old’s declaration of parental approval before enabling processing under the service’s standard consent procedure.
Notify the parent about intended collection before enabling processing, with a subsequent opportunity to object provided.
Document the educational purpose before enabling processing, treating the learning context as sufficient grounds for exemption.
scenes.plot: A sixteen-year-old accepts the new terms on a tablet. The account profile lists no parent or guardian contact.
scenes.good: The adult’s identity and age are checked appropriately before parental consent is relied on.
scenes.effect: A sixteen-year-old’s click stands in for adult consent. A checkbox has not become a parent.

scenes.q: The guardian cannot use the only accepted form with a keyboard. Which support change actually allows the rights request to proceed?
scenes.a: Provide an accessible private submission route with clear guidance, allowing the guardian’s rights request to proceed.
scenes.why: The Act provides rights including access, correction, erasure and grievance redressal. The Rules require the notice to describe means to exercise those rights and make complaints.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, ss. 11–13; DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 3(c)
bad: Provide detailed submission instructions with clear guidance, retaining the existing form as the required completion route.
Provide a public support thread with staff assistance, allowing the guardian to submit verification documents there.
Provide private email assistance with form completion, accepting the request once the existing form is submitted.
scenes.plot: A guardian asks to correct a child’s profile, but the only request form is unreadable with assistive technology and rejects keyboard navigation.
scenes.good: The guardian can use an accessible rights channel without broadcasting the child’s details.
scenes.effect: A guardian cannot exercise rights. An inaccessible form is a locked door with a help icon.

speaker: NILA / SAFETY
brief: A learning game turns children into ad segments. Find the tracker, check the parent, fix the rights desk.
joke: Children learn maths. The ad network learns the children.

title: The Vendor at 02:14

scenes.q: The reminder vendor offers an NDA but also asks to keep a research copy. Which approval package should the startup require?
scenes.a: Require a processing contract and safeguards for reminders, withholding research-copy approval until its separate basis exists.
scenes.why: A Data Fiduciary may engage a Data Processor under a valid contract, but remains responsible for compliance with the Act in respect of processing undertaken by it or on its behalf.
bad: Require a confidentiality agreement and safeguards for reminders, allowing the research copy within the confidentiality restrictions.
Require a restricted initial transfer and safeguards for reminders, completing the processing contract after access begins.
Require a processing contract and safeguards for reminders, assigning the company’s statutory responsibility exclusively to vendors.
scenes.plot: A reminder vendor needs names and phone numbers to send appointment messages. Its sales lead asks to keep a copy for unrelated product research.
scenes.good: A valid contract limits reminder processing and protects customer details.
scenes.effect: Customer numbers are shared on a handshake. The vendor can drift beyond the appointment purpose.

scenes.q: The primary processor vouches for a new subcontractor, but its identifiable-event access has not been reviewed. What should happen before access begins?
scenes.a: Review purpose, contractual coverage and safeguards before authorizing subcontractor access to the identifiable customer event stream.
scenes.why: The Data Fiduciary remains responsible for processing on its behalf and must use reasonable security safeguards. Vendor access should be governed by a valid contract and the purpose disclosed to the Data Principal.
bad: Approve confidential subcontractor access under an NDA, reviewing contractual coverage after the planned service release completes.
Approve subcontractor access following the primary processor’s recommendation, treating its selection as confirmation of authorized processing.
Approve subcontractor access after hashing customer identifiers, treating pseudonymisation as sufficient grounds to waive further review.
scenes.plot: The analytics processor proposes a subcontractor that will see identifiable events. The release is already scheduled and the contract owner is offline.
scenes.good: Subcontractor access waits until purpose, contract and safeguards are checked.
scenes.effect: Identifiable events reach an unchecked subcontractor. An NDA cannot legitimise unrestricted reuse.

scenes.q: The vendor caused the incident and signed an indemnity. Who must still ensure the company’s Data Fiduciary duties are met?
scenes.a: The company retains responsibility for processing on its behalf, while the vendor performs agreed operational duties.
scenes.why: Section 8(1) places responsibility on the Data Fiduciary for compliance with the Act in respect of processing undertaken by it or on its behalf, including through a processor.
bad: The company retains responsibility for incident notices, while the vendor assumes all remaining statutory processing duties.
The company assumes responsibility after a customer complaint, while the vendor manages compliance until that point.
The company transfers responsibility through the indemnity clause, while the vendor manages compliance for outsourced processing.
scenes.plot: After a vendor incident, executives say the processor caused it, so the company has no responsibility. The response channel is waiting for an owner.
scenes.good: The fiduciary owns its duties while coordinating the vendor response.
scenes.effect: Response stalls while everyone blames the processor. The fiduciary’s statutory duties remain.

speaker: RAFI / ENGINEERING
brief: An appointment vendor brings a subcontractor and a convenient theory of responsibility.
joke: The vendor says they own the problem. Their contract says they own a beanbag.

title: The Red Light at 02:31

scenes.q: The personal drive is still syncing and the extent is unknown. Which response covers the immediate exposure and the duties that follow?
scenes.a: Stop the sync, investigate affected copies, restore safeguards and initiate the applicable breach notification response process.
scenes.why: Data Fiduciaries must take reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breaches. If a breach occurs, they must notify the Board and affected Data Principals in the prescribed manner.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 8(5)–(6); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 7
bad: Stop the sync, delete the local copy, restore safeguards and close the incident following containment actions.
Secure the account, investigate affected copies, restore safeguards and defer notices until complete forensic findings arrive.
Refer containment to the provider, restore account access and accept its standard communications as completing notifications.
scenes.plot: An employee exported customer records to a personal drive. The drive is still syncing, and nobody can confirm how many copies exist.
scenes.good: The sync is contained; evidence is preserved and breach duties are assessed.
scenes.effect: Exposure continues or evidence disappears. The team loses the means to understand and contain the breach.

scenes.q: The provider says it will handle notices but offers no completion evidence. Which responsibility should your incident owner retain?
scenes.a: Retain oversight of required Board and affected-person notices, verifying that delegated delivery meets the prescribed requirements.
scenes.why: A Data Fiduciary remains responsible for processing undertaken by it or on its behalf, including by a Data Processor. Section 8(6) requires notice of a personal data breach to the Board and each affected Data Principal.
bad: Delegate required notices to the provider’s incident team, recording its assurance as completion of notification duties.
Verify delivery of required Board notices, allowing the provider to decide whether affected people need notification.
Verify restoration of the provider’s security safeguards, treating completed remediation as sufficient grounds to close notifications.
scenes.plot: A cloud provider reports that records held for the company were exposed. Its support agent says the vendor will handle every notice.
scenes.good: The fiduciary owns notification compliance instead of assuming the cloud vendor will.
scenes.effect: People wait while vendor and company point at each other. Outsourcing storage did not outsource accountability.

scenes.q: Communications wants certainty before speaking; forensics is incomplete. Which notification plan should you authorize now?
scenes.a: Issue required initial notices without delay, sharing available facts and supplying further details through prescribed updates.
scenes.why: Rule 7 requires initial notice to the Board and each affected person without delay. Updated details go to the Board within 72 hours of awareness, or a longer period it allows on written request. Reputational discomfort is not an exception.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 8(6); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 7
bad: Issue initial notices within the later update window, using that interval to gather the outstanding facts.
Issue the initial Board notice without delay, contacting affected people after forensic analysis confirms complete details.
Issue affected-person notices without delay, contacting the Board after the final assessment establishes substantial resulting harm.
scenes.plot: The incident commander wants to wait until every detail is certain; communications worries that a notice will damage trust.
scenes.good: Initial notices start without delay; detailed Board information follows within 72 hours unless extended on written request.
scenes.effect: People lose time to protect themselves. The 72-hour detail window is not permission to delay initial notices.

speaker: RAFI / RESPONSE
brief: A personal drive becomes a breach. Contain it and get the truth to affected people.
joke: Someone named the folder FINAL_secure_v7. The folder took that personally.

title: The Rights Desk After Hours

scenes.q: Identity checks are complete. The user asked for their processing summary, not the general policy. Which response satisfies the request?
scenes.a: Provide the required account-specific processing information, using the completed identity checks to progress the access request.
scenes.why: A Data Principal has a right to obtain a summary of personal data being processed and the processing activities, subject to the Act and prescribed manner.
bad: Provide the current privacy policy describing processing, using the completed identity checks to close the request.
Provide the stored profile fields without processing details, using the completed identity checks to complete responses.
Provide instructions for obtaining judicial authorization, using the completed identity checks to prepare the eventual disclosure.
scenes.plot: A user asks for a summary of the personal data and the processing activities tied to their account. The support script offers only a privacy-policy link.
scenes.good: The verified requester gets the summary they are entitled to, without another person’s records.
scenes.effect: A policy link replaces the summary. The user still cannot understand their actual processing.

scenes.q: The misspelling is verified and the record remains in use. Which action resolves the request instead of merely recording a ticket?
scenes.a: Update the verified name in active processing records, recording the correction and confirming resolution with customers.
scenes.why: The Act grants the Data Principal a right to correction, completion and updating of personal data, in accordance with applicable requirements.
bad: Record the verified name in the correction queue, retaining existing processing records until the annual review.
Update the verified name in the customer interface, retaining existing names in the operational processing records.
Prepare the verified name correction for processing, applying it once the customer withdraws unrelated service consent.
scenes.plot: A customer shows that their profile misspells their name. A support agent says profile changes are locked until the next annual review.
scenes.good: The inaccurate name can be corrected through the rights process.
scenes.effect: A known error follows the person. Annual release cycles do not justify refusing a valid request.

scenes.q: The deletion ticket went unanswered. Which grievance route should the service provide before sending the customer elsewhere?
scenes.a: Provide accessible internal redress with an assigned owner, timely responses and Board escalation after internal exhaustion.
scenes.why: Data Fiduciaries must establish an effective mechanism to redress grievances. Data Principals must exhaust the opportunity to raise a grievance with the Data Fiduciary or Consent Manager before approaching the Board.
bad: Provide an accessible complaint address with receipt tracking, allowing individual teams to decide ownership after submission.
Provide direct Board referral with supporting ticket details, routing unresolved requests externally before offering internal redress.
Provide internal redress with an assigned owner, activating the grievance process after the customer closes accounts.
scenes.plot: A deletion request went unanswered. The customer now wants to file a grievance, but the product team cannot find a complaint owner.
scenes.good: An accessible grievance mechanism gets an owner; the person can approach the Board after exhausting it.
scenes.effect: The complaint has no useful path. Support keeps generating apologies while the problem escalates.

speaker: ASHA / SUPPORT
brief: A missing data summary leads to a wrong name and an unanswered complaint. Make the desk work for people.
joke: The bot apologised 46 times. This is apology-as-a-service.

title: The Memory Drawer

scenes.q: The event purpose has ended and extra profiles remain in staging and processor systems. Which cleanup plan accounts for the remaining copies?
scenes.a: Erase unnecessary company and processor copies, retaining only records covered by an identified legal retention requirement.
scenes.why: The Data Fiduciary must erase personal data when consent is withdrawn or the specified purpose is no longer served, unless retention is required by law. Check applicable minimum retention rules before erasing processing records.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 8(7); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 8(3)
bad: Erase unnecessary company copies and document completion, leaving processor copies available under their existing storage arrangements.
Archive company and processor copies under legal hold, identifying the specific retention requirement during subsequent review.
Remove account identifiers from company and processor copies, retaining other identifiable profile details for operational reference.
scenes.plot: The ticketing service finished an event months ago. Extra attendee profile data remains in a staging bucket with no owner.
scenes.good: Unneeded extras and processor copies are erased after applicable retention requirements are checked.
scenes.effect: Unused profiles enlarge the breach surface, or mandatory records are deleted without checking retention duties.

scenes.q: No law requires these dietary preferences, although some processing records have retention requirements. Which deletion decision is justified?
scenes.a: Erase the dietary preferences after purpose completion, preserving separately required records within their applicable retention periods.
scenes.why: Section 8(7) requires erasure when the specified purpose is no longer served unless retention is necessary for compliance with law. Rule 8 also sets specified erasure periods and requires at least one year of certain processing data and logs for purposes in the Seventh Schedule.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 8(7); DPDP Rules, 2025, r. 8(1)–(3)
bad: Encrypt the dietary preferences after purpose completion, preserving them for potential reuse during a future event.
Retain the dietary preferences with processing logs, applying the log-retention requirement across the complete attendee profile.
Archive the dietary preferences under restricted access, treating removal from the active database as completed erasure.
scenes.plot: A one-time event is over and no law requires keeping dietary preferences. Operations wants to retain them in case the event returns.
scenes.good: Purpose-ended data is erased when no law requires retention; legally required records are separated.
scenes.effect: An archive excuses indefinite reuse, or legally required records are erased too soon.

scenes.q: Two credible records conflict and the lender’s decision job is about to run. Which plan addresses the unresolved accuracy risk before it affects the person?
scenes.a: Pause the decision and reconcile conflicting records, checking completeness, accuracy and consistency before resuming the assessment.
scenes.why: Where personal data is likely to be used to make a decision affecting a Data Principal or disclosed to another Data Fiduciary, the Data Fiduciary must ensure completeness, accuracy and consistency.
bad: Run the decision and flag conflicting records, initiating reconciliation if the customer subsequently challenges the assessment.
Select the newer timestamped record, treating its recency as sufficient resolution of the conflicting customer information.
Ask the vendor to reconcile conflicting records, allowing queued decisions to proceed while confirmation remains outstanding.
scenes.plot: A lender finds contradictory profile records just before using them for a decision that affects a customer. The scoring job is queued.
scenes.good: Conflicting records are reconciled before a decision affecting the person.
scenes.effect: Contradictory data drives a consequential decision. The fastest record is not necessarily accurate.

speaker: DEV / RECORDS
brief: Old profiles, lingering copies and a contradictory loan record. Decide what to keep, erase and correct.
joke: We retain everything forever. It’s cheaper than deciding what anything is for.

title: The Borderless Copy

scenes.q: The migration approver must decide whether an overseas region can be used. Which checks are necessary before treating the transfer as permitted?
scenes.a: Check destination restrictions, applicable transfer directions and stricter sector requirements before approving the proposed overseas migration.
scenes.why: The Act authorizes transfer of personal data outside India subject to restrictions the Central Government may specify, and does not override stricter restrictions under other Indian laws.
scenes.law: DPDP Act, 2023, s. 16; DPDP Rules 2025, r. 15
bad: Check destination restrictions and provider safeguards before approving migration, treating sector requirements as covered by checks.
Obtain specific customer consent and provider safeguards before approving migration, treating consent as overriding destination restrictions.
Review provider reputation and contractual safeguards before approving migration, treating those assurances as establishing transfer eligibility.
scenes.plot: A service wants to move account data to a cloud region outside India. The engineer says the Act bans every overseas transfer.
scenes.good: The team checks notified transfer restrictions, Rule 15 requirements and stricter sector laws.
scenes.effect: The team invents a universal ban or ignores actual restrictions. Either derails a lawful transfer assessment.

scenes.q: The vendor found a public page but cannot establish who posted it. Which assessment is needed before combining those profiles with the account copy?
scenes.a: Establish who published the data and whether exclusion applies before determining a basis for combining profiles.
scenes.why: The Act excludes certain personal data made or caused to be made publicly available by the Data Principal or under a legal obligation, but the facts and statutory conditions matter.
bad: Establish that the page requires no login before treating its visible contents as excluded personal data.
Obtain the vendor’s confirmation of public accessibility before treating the discovered profile as meeting exclusion conditions.
Verify consent for the existing private account before treating that agreement as authorization for public-profile combination.
scenes.plot: A vendor finds profile details on a public page and proposes combining them with the overseas account copy. The source and the person who posted it are unclear.
scenes.good: The source is checked: the public-data exclusion depends on who made it public and why.
scenes.effect: Public visibility is mistaken for permission. A leaked list was not made public by its Data Principals.

scenes.q: The cloud help desk cannot answer for your service’s processing. Which contact arrangement should replace the incomplete help page?
scenes.a: Publish business contact details for someone authorized to answer the service’s processing questions and rights requests.
scenes.why: The Act requires a Data Fiduciary to publish the business contact information of its Data Protection Officer, if applicable, or another person able to answer questions on its behalf.
bad: Publish the cloud provider’s support details for processing questions, relying on its infrastructure expertise when responding.
Assign an internal privacy owner for processing questions, maintaining contact details within the service’s internal directory.
Publish the sales team’s contact details for processing questions, relying on its existing customer communication role.
scenes.plot: A user asks who can explain the processing and how to raise a concern. The help page lists the cloud vendor but no responsible contact.
scenes.good: A responsible business contact can answer processing and rights questions.
scenes.effect: Users reach a cloud vendor instead of a responsible contact. Accountability becomes a forwarding loop.

speaker: NILA / INFRA
brief: A cloud migration meets a public-data shortcut. Follow the source, destination and responsible contact.
joke: The cloud is someone else’s computer. The spreadsheet calls it a jurisdiction.

title: The Audit Trail Nobody Budgeted For

scenes.q: The export contains only a timestamp. Which evidence should the reviewer be able to connect to the specific purpose and user action?
scenes.a: Link the actual notice version, stated purpose and affirmative consent action to the recorded interaction timestamp.
scenes.why: The Data Fiduciary bears the burden of proving that notice was given and consent was obtained in accordance with the Act when consent is relied upon.
bad: Link the current notice version, stated purpose and recorded timestamp as evidence of earlier consent interaction.
Link the general terms acceptance and recorded timestamp as evidence of consent for the processing purpose.
Link a reconstructed notice screen and recorded timestamp, presenting the reconstruction as evidence of original interaction.
scenes.plot: A reviewer asks how one user agreed to a specific data use. The team can find a timestamp but not the notice or action shown at the time.
scenes.good: Notice and affirmative consent evidence support the permission being relied upon.
scenes.effect: The team cannot demonstrate agreement. Reconstructed confidence is not a consent record.

scenes.q: The correction documents appear to belong to another person. Which handling approach addresses authenticity without creating another disclosure?
scenes.a: Resolve the identity mismatch using authentic information, restricting document access while checking the requested correction privately.
scenes.why: Data Principals have duties under section 15, including furnishing only verifiably authentic information when exercising rights and not impersonating another person.
scenes.law: DPDP Act 2023, s. 15(b), (e); secure verification supports rights handling
bad: Accept the correction using supplied documents, treating further identity checks as an obstacle to exercising rights.
Classify the mismatch as established impersonation, distributing the supplied documents across operational teams for immediate awareness.
Confirm the account exists using internal records, treating that confirmation as sufficient verification of correction requests.
scenes.plot: A correction request arrives with documents that appear to belong to someone else. A manager wants to publish them in the team chat to expose the fraud.
scenes.good: The request is verified proportionately, requiring authentic information without public shaming.
scenes.effect: Impersonation succeeds or documents are exposed in retaliation. Neither is appropriate verification.

scenes.q: The intern needs ticket status, but both the UI and API permit full customer exports. Which access change actually reduces the unnecessary authorization?
scenes.a: Revoke unnecessary UI and API export permissions, retaining ticket-status access and appropriate safeguards for intern duties.
scenes.why: Reasonable security safeguards are required to protect personal data. Limiting unnecessary access reduces the likelihood and impact of unauthorized disclosure.
bad: Retain UI and API export permissions with monitoring, adding usage restrictions and alerts for unusual activity.
Disable customer exports within the user interface, retaining API export permission for continuity of operational integrations.
Require stronger authentication for UI and API access, retaining existing export permissions within the assigned role.
scenes.plot: The audit finds that a support intern can download every customer record, though the role needs only ticket status. The access review is overdue.
scenes.good: Role-appropriate access replaces broad downloads, with safeguards and logs.
scenes.effect: The intern can still export the customer base. Convenience has become a breach multiplier.
